teaser: A saint holds up his own skin. The face on it belongs to the painter.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo shows the altar wall in place, at a slight angle, with parts of the side walls and ceiling; the fresco fills roughly x 0.15 to 0.80. Figures are small, so interactive blocks point only at large groups that are legible. Minos (bottom right corner) is told in text but not pointed at because the corner is too dark here.
Self-portrait in Bartholomew's skin: first proposed by Francesco La Cava in 1925, widely accepted, not documented.
Dates 1536 to 1541; wall about 13.7 x 12 m; more than 300 figures (often given as about 390).
Biagio da Cesena anecdote and the pope's reply come from Vasari.
Decision to cover the nudes January 1564; Daniele da Volterra worked in 1565; Saint Catherine (and Saint Blaise) were repainted by him.
Restoration of this wall 1990 to 1994 kept Daniele's additions and removed some later ones: check.
Ultramarine from lapis lazuli used for the sky: check.

lesson.text: Somewhere on this wall a man sits on a cloud, bald, gray-bearded, powerfully built, and whole. In his left hand he dangles a human skin, peeled off in one piece. It is supposed to be his own. But the face hanging from that skin is beardless, dark-haired and nothing like his.

The man is Saint Bartholomew, who according to tradition was skinned alive for his faith. Saints in paintings carry the tool of their death the way we carry an ID card. He has the knife and the skin. So whose face did Michelangelo put on it?

lesson.title: Two faces
lesson.text: He sits just below and to the right of the central figure.

spots.title: The saint
spots.text: Bartholomew twists on his cloud and looks up, as if asking a question of the figure above. His body is intact: on the last day, the dead get their bodies back.

spots.title: The skin
spots.text: A limp gray sack with empty arms and a sagging, distorted face. Since 1925 most scholars have recognized that face as Michelangelo's own. It is the only self-portrait he ever put in paint.

lesson.text: A self-portrait as an empty hide, held over the pit of hell by a saint who may or may not let go. Michelangelo was in his sixties, deeply religious and anxious about his soul. In poems from these years he wrote about his sins and his fear of dying unforgiven.

He had come back to the Sistine Chapel almost 25 years after finishing its ceiling. Pope Clement VII asked for the wall behind the altar. Clement died, and Paul III insisted. Michelangelo worked alone on it from 1536 to 1541, on a surface about 13.7 by 12 meters (45 by 40 ft).

To get one unbroken surface, earlier art was destroyed: frescoes by Perugino, two windows that were bricked up, and two arched scenes Michelangelo himself had painted at the top of the wall while working on the ceiling.

The subject is the end of time. Christ returns, the dead climb out of the earth, and every soul is sent up or down. Painters usually arranged this in neat rows, like a courtroom. Michelangelo painted more than 300 bodies in a single sky, with no frame and no floor. Yet the crowd moves in an order.
Remember that the fresco is the blue area in the middle of this photo. Three lines show how the crowd turns.

lines.label: Rising
lines.text: On the left, the dead leave the ground at the bottom, float up through the air, and join the crowd of the saved around Christ.

lines.label: The gesture
lines.text: Christ's right arm is raised above his head, his left crosses his chest. He does not sit in judgment. He is half standing, and the whole wall seems to turn around that arm.

lines.label: Falling
lines.text: On the right, bodies are pushed back down, wrestled by angels and dragged by demons toward the boat and the red glow in the bottom corner.

lesson.text: The wall works like a slow wheel: up on Christ's right, down on his left, with his raised arm as the hub. One gesture sets hundreds of bodies in motion.

This Christ surprised people. He has no beard and the torso of a Greek athlete, closer to an ancient statue of Apollo than to the gentle figure of older paintings. Mary, tucked against his side, turns her head away. Even the saints look uneasy. Nobody here is sure of the verdict.

The blue is ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, a stone carried to Italy from the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. It was among the costliest colors a painter could use, and here it covers the whole sky. The pope was paying.

There are no wings on the angels and no halos on the saints. Everyone is simply a body, and when the wall was unveiled in 1541 nearly all of them were naked. For Michelangelo the nude was the most serious subject in art. For others, in the pope's own chapel, it was a scandal.

The pope's master of ceremonies, Biagio da Cesena, said the picture belonged in a tavern. Michelangelo painted him into the bottom right corner as Minos, judge of hell, with donkey's ears. When Biagio complained, the pope reportedly joked that his power did not reach into hell.

The critics won in the end. In 1564, weeks before Michelangelo died at 88, the Church decided the nudity had to be covered. A painter who admired him, Daniele da Volterra, added cloths and loincloths. It earned Daniele a nickname for life: “the breeches maker.”

Much of that cloth is still there, kept as part of the wall's history when it was cleaned in the 1990s. Now roam the photo yourself. The details are small at this distance, so the markers point to whole groups.

spots.title: Christ and Mary
spots.text: He is ringed by a pale yellow glow. She sits close in pink and blue, knees drawn up, face turned down toward the saved. She no longer pleads: the time for that is over.

spots.title: A giant on the left
spots.text: This huge standing nude, usually identified as John the Baptist, is among the largest figures on the wall. Michelangelo made the upper figures bigger so they read from the floor.

spots.title: Catherine's wheel
spots.text: A woman bends over a broken wheel, the tool of her martyrdom. She was painted nude. Her green dress is one of Daniele da Volterra's additions, and he repainted the saint behind her too.

spots.title: The trumpets
spots.text: Wingless angels blow long trumpets to wake the dead. Two of them hold open books: a small one for the names of the saved, and a much larger one for the damned.

spots.title: The man who understands
spots.text: A lone figure covers half his face with one hand while demons pull him down by the legs. He does not fight. He stares out with one eye, realizing where he is going.

spots.title: The dead wake
spots.text: On a strip of bare earth, bodies crawl out of the ground, some still wrapped in shrouds, some little more than skeletons putting flesh back on.

spots.title: The boat
spots.text: A dark ferryman swings an oar to drive the damned out of his boat. He is Charon, borrowed from Greek myth by way of the poet Dante, whom Michelangelo knew almost by heart.

spots.title: The cross
spots.text: In the arched top of the wall, angels struggle to carry the cross. On the other side they carry the column where Christ was whipped: the evidence for the trial.

lesson.text: The room is still in use. When a pope dies, the cardinals lock themselves in this chapel to elect the next one, and they cast their votes facing this wall. Each man walks toward the judging Christ with his ballot. A few steps to the right hangs a painter's empty skin, still waiting to hear.

quiz.question: Whose face is thought to appear on the skin held by Saint Bartholomew?
quiz.explanation: Since 1925 most scholars have read the sagging face as a self-portrait.

quiz.question: How does the crowd move across the wall?
options: Up on the left, down on the right
From right to left in rows
quiz.explanation: The saved rise on Christ's right and the damned fall on his left, like a slow wheel.

quiz.question: What was unusual about this Christ?
options: He is shown as a child
He is beardless and built like an ancient athlete
quiz.explanation: He resembles a statue of Apollo more than the gentle Christ of older paintings.

quiz.question: Why was Daniele da Volterra called “the breeches maker”?
options: He painted cloth over the nude figures
He was a tailor before he was a painter
He designed costumes for the pope
quiz.explanation: After 1564 he added draperies and loincloths to the fresco.

quiz.question: What do the trumpeting angels hold besides trumpets?
options: Two books, a small one and a large one
quiz.explanation: The small book lists the saved, the larger one the damned.

quiz.question: Where does the blue of the sky come from?
options: Lapis lazuli, a stone from far to the east
quiz.explanation: Ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli and was among the costliest colors.

facts.text: Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment at the same time as the Sistine ceiling.
facts.explanation: He returned to the chapel almost 25 years after finishing the ceiling.

facts.text: Michelangelo painted a papal official who criticized him as a judge of hell with donkey's ears.
facts.explanation: Biagio da Cesena became Minos in the bottom right corner.

facts.text: The angels on this wall have large feathered wings.
facts.explanation: The angels have no wings and the saints have no halos.
